strings.hist.soviet.repatriation.title: Forced repatriations after Yalta
strings.hist.soviet.repatriation.text: In February 1945, at Yalta, the Allies agreed on the return of liberated Soviet citizens. By the end of September 1945 the Western Allies had handed over more than two million people to the USSR. Most wanted to go home. But tens of thousands were handed over against their will: above all men from units in German service, often with their families, and also émigrés who had never been Soviet citizens. Near Lienz in East Tyrol, people died in June 1945, some by their own hand, when British soldiers forcibly cleared the Cossack camps. The last forced repatriations ran in 1946/47 as “Operation Keelhaul”. The NKVD screened all returnees in filtration camps; hundreds of thousands ended up in prison or forced labour. In the West this only became widely known in the 1970s.
strings.hist.soviet.handover_1940.title: Handed over by the NKVD to the Gestapo
strings.hist.soviet.handover_1940.text: From 1937 the USSR expelled arrested Germans and Austrians. After the partition of Poland in 1939 the two dictatorships shared a border: from December 1939 the NKVD handed the expellees, mostly inmates of prisons and camps, directly to German authorities, above all on the Bug bridge at Brest-Litovsk – probably several hundred people by May 1941. Many had fled the Nazi regime, among them communists and Jews. In February 1940 it was Margarete Buber-Neumann’s turn. Her partner, the former KPD leader Heinz Neumann, had been arrested in Moscow in 1937 and shot; she herself had been held in the Karaganda camp in Kazakhstan. After Gestapo custody she was sent to Ravensbrück concentration camp in August 1940 and remained there until April 1945. In 1949 her account “Als Gefangene bei Stalin und Hitler” was published.
strings.hist.reich.nuremberg_interpreters.title: Simultaneous interpreting at the Nuremberg trial
strings.hist.reich.nuremberg_interpreters.text: At the trial of the major war criminals before the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg (20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946), simultaneous interpreting was used on a large scale for the first time, between English, French, Russian and German. Through the headphones of an IBM system, judges, prosecution, defence, defendants and press heard every word in their own language by turning a selector switch. Three teams of twelve interpreters each took turns, in booths glazed at the front and sides and open at the top. A monitoring interpreter used a yellow lamp to ask speakers to slow down and a red one to ask them to pause. In this way documents, films and witness testimony about the Nazi crimes, about mass murder and the extermination camps, could be presented and examined in four languages at once.
